claimText: I found a $340 charge on my card from an online electronics store I've never heard of and never shopped at. My physical card has been in my wallet the whole time. I have never bought anything from this merchant before, ever.
note: Clean fraud claim: card-absent, unauthorized, no prior merchant relationship - matches 10.4's definition with none of the disqualifying factors the policy names.

claimText: Someone used my card number to buy a $600 digital gift card from a website I've never visited in my life. I don't recognize the merchant name at all and have zero purchase history with them.
note: Second clean 10.4 case, deliberately different phrasing (gift card, not electronics) to check the classifier isn't just pattern-matching one surface wording.

claimText: I paid for a couch three weeks ago. It was supposed to arrive last Friday. It's now five days late, tracking hasn't updated in over a week, and the seller isn't responding. I want my money back.
note: Clean 13.1: nothing was ever delivered, past the expected delivery date.

claimText: I ordered a birthday gift two weeks ago for a delivery that was guaranteed by yesterday. The order still shows 'processing' and has never shipped. The event has already passed.
note: Second clean 13.1 case with different phrasing (never shipped at all, vs. claim-03's stalled-in-transit framing).

claimText: The blender I ordered was advertised as 1000 watts with ten speed settings. What actually arrived is a much smaller, generic-looking blender with only three speeds, and the lid is cracked.
note: Clean 13.3: something was received, but it materially differs from its description.

claimText: My new phone case arrived visibly cracked down one side and the clasp is snapped off. It's unusable straight out of the box.
note: Second clean 13.3 case - defective on arrival, rather than claim-05's wrong-product framing, to cover both halves of 13.3's definition.

claimText: I ordered a specific laptop model. What showed up is a completely different, cheaper laptop with lower specs than what I paid for and what the listing described.
note: Genuinely ambiguous: the laptop that was ordered was never received (arguing for 13.1), but a physical item was delivered that materially differs from the description (arguing for 13.3). The policy text doesn't resolve wrong-item-delivered as clearly belonging to one code over the other. A good classifier should surface this tension rather than confidently pick one without justification.

claimText: I don't recognize a $210 charge on my statement and never authorized it - though now that I look closer, I did buy something from this exact same online store about a month ago.
note: The customer's own framing is textbook 10.4 (unauthorized charge), but the disclosed prior purchase from the same merchant is precisely the disqualifying pattern the policy names: 'a pattern of prior legitimate purchases materially weakens a fraud claim and may result in the dispute being declined before it is ever filed.' A classifier that just pattern-matches 'I didn't authorize this' to 10.4 without registering that caveat is missing the actual point of retrieving the policy text at all - this case tests whether retrieval is doing real work or just decoration.
